entries.description: a `function` declaration or function expression with a default-valued parameter (arrow forms excluded -- they fail closed)

a call whose callee identifier resolves to a `let`/`var` binding, a parameter, or a `const` aliasing another name, rather than to a function declaration or a `const` bound directly to a function literal
a `.forEach(...)` call with any callback, or a `.filter(...)` call whose callback is an expression-bodied arrow
a call to any `console` sink with two or more arguments where at least one argument is not a literal or a substitution-free template
an object literal property whose value is a function expression or arrow function (shorthand methods excluded -- they fail closed)

a `switch` statement with at least one following sibling statement, inside a function body or nested block -- a top-level `switch` is harmless, since the damage is reparenting the remaining statements INTO module scope and they are already there
an optional call `f?.(...)`
a C-style `for` that omits a clause in any arity the count-based classifier misreads -- every omission except `for(;test;)`, `for(init;test;)` and `for(;;)`
a `var` or `let` declarator whose initializer is an object literal or an array literal
a `const` declarator whose initializer is not a literal -- an identifier, binary, unary, parenthesized, conditional, member or call expression

an `==`/`!=`/`===`/`!==` comparison with a `null`, `undefined`, boolean-literal or numeric-literal operand, or any `??` expression; upper bound, since the 2026-07-19 fix closed the provable majority and the surviving residuals are gated on the compiler failing to prove the other operand's type class -- a compiler-internal decision the AST cannot see
a `continue` whose innermost enclosing loop is a C-style `for` with an update clause, a `do...while`, or a `for...in`
a let/const declaration in a nested block whose declared name is also bound in an enclosing scope

a computed element store to an array-literal binding on either silent lane -- through an alias declarator (`const b = a; b[0] = ...`) in either scope, or un-aliased at module scope (the un-aliased in-function form fails closed E5506, so scope, not the declarator, is the discriminator there)
computed member access whose key expression is not a literal
a member or computed read applied directly to a call expression's result

an indexed element read of a `.split(...)` call whose receiver, separator argument and index are ALL literals -- i.e. the whole access folds statically -- used as a `+` concat operand; residual R-A4-4, the only surviving silent lane now that the runtime `.split` lane fails closed E5506

a `.slice(...)`, `.charAt(...)`, `.toUpperCase(...)` or `.repeat(...)` call used as a `+` concat operand (`.substring(...)` excluded -- it is correct, as is every non-concat position); upper bound, since the AST cannot see that the receiver is a runtime string

entries.reason: a representation condition of the same G5 family as R-16 -- a string handle reaching a consumer that never proved it was a string; whether an array element or `Object.keys` result is a string is a repr fact, not a syntactic one

entries.description: a `&&` or `||` whose left operand is a string literal
a call to `String(...)` or to a `.toString()` method, including the computed `["toString"]()` spelling
a call to `JSON.stringify(...)`, including the computed `JSON["stringify"](...)` spelling

entries.reason: a representation condition -- there is no `undefined` distinct from scalar `0`, so it fires wherever an expression *evaluates* to absent or void (a missing field, an out-of-range read, a void return), which is a runtime-value fact rather than a construct in the source

a runtime-type condition -- the missing rung is number/string coercion, so it fires only when the two operands actually hold a number and a string at run time; same-type `==` comparisons are correct, and the operator alone does not identify the case

entries.description: a `typeof` whose operand is not a bare literal
a call to `Object.freeze(...)` or `Object.isFrozen(...)` whose argument is an already-bound identifier rather than an inline literal
an array literal containing a spread element

a unary `+` whose operand is not a numeric literal -- a string literal, identifier, member or call expression; upper bound, since the defect needs the operand to hold a non-numeric string at run time, which the AST cannot see (`+"42"`, `+"-5"`, `+"1.5"`, `+""` and `+true` are correct)
a sequence (comma) expression in value position
a unary `-` applied to the numeric literal `0`
a `for...of` whose iterable is an identifier declared by `let` with an array-literal initializer
an assignment of an array to an object field that the object literal initialized with a numeric literal
a `for...of` with a `var` or `let` loop variable whose iterable is an array literal
an assignment whose target is an identifier declared `const` in an enclosing scope

entries.reason: only invalid JavaScript triggers it -- acorn, like node, rejects a second `default` clause as a SyntaxError, so the shape can never appear in a corpus file that parses

entries.description: a single-argument direct `console.log` whose argument is any boolean producer other than an inline `true`/`false` literal -- a comparison, `!`/`!!`, `&&`/`||`, a conditional, a literal-selecting `??` (one whose statically-selected operand is a boolean literal; a `??` over an unprovable operand is R-08 residual 6, not this entry), a call to a user function, a parameter read, a `var`-bound identifier, or a `const` object-field read (a plain `const` scalar binding is excluded -- it now renders correctly); upper bound, since for the call, parameter, `var`-binding and object-field producers the AST cannot see whether the value is actually a boolean -- the literal-selecting `??` is not among them, being decidable from the operands themselves
a `console.log` argument, or a `+` concat operand, that is an array or object literal or an identifier bound to one
a numeric literal whose magnitude is at least 1e21, or is nonzero and below 1e-6
a call to `console.warn(...)`
a call to a user function whose `return` yields a comparison, `!`, or logical expression, used as a `+` concat operand or as a non-first `console.log` argument
